The van't Hoff factor compares what the solution actually does with what one mole of
undissociated solute would do.
i = observed ΔTf / calculated ΔTf
i = 0.0205 / 0.0197 = 1.041
So the particles outnumber the formula units slightly — acetic acid is only partly ionised.
CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻, so one particle becomes two and n = 2.
Degree of dissociation: α = (i − 1)/(n − 1)
α = (1.041 − 1)/(2 − 1) = 0.041
That is about 4% ionised, which is what you expect of a weak acid.
∴ i = 1.041 and α = 0.041.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|52||0|0.s:
By Raoult's law the relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute:
(p° − p)/p° = χsolute
Moles of urea = mass / molar mass = 18 / 60 = 0.3 mol.
Moles of water = 100 / 18 = 5.556 mol.
χurea = 0.3 / (0.3 + 5.556) = 0.3 / 5.856 = 0.0512
Note the solvent moles must be counted in the total; dividing by 5.556 alone would give 0.054.
∴ the relative lowering is about 0.05.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|54||0|0.s:
Kohlrausch's law says a limiting molar conductivity is the sum of independent ionic contributions,
so you can add and subtract whole electrolytes to manufacture the pair of ions you want.
The target is Λ°(NH₄OH) = λ°(NH₄⁺) + λ°(OH⁻).
NH₄OH is a weak base, so this cannot be measured directly — hence the trick.
Take Λ°(NH₄Cl) + Λ°(NaOH) − Λ°(NaCl):
= [λ(NH₄⁺) + λ(Cl⁻)] + [λ(Na⁺) + λ(OH⁻)] − [λ(Na⁺) + λ(Cl⁻)]
The Na⁺ terms cancel and the Cl⁻ terms cancel.
= λ(NH₄⁺) + λ(OH⁻)
∴ Λ°(NH₄OH) = Λ°(NH₄Cl) + Λ°(NaOH) − Λ°(NaCl).

kcet|Chemistry|2026|55||0|0.s:
Split the target reaction 3Mn²⁺ ⇒ Mn + 2Mn³⁺ into its two halves.
Reduction (cathode): Mn²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇒ Mn, E° = −1.18 V, used as given.
Oxidation (anode): 2Mn²⁺ ⇒ 2Mn³⁺ + 2e⁻, which is the reverse of Mn³⁺ + e⁻ ⇒ Mn²⁺, E° = +1.51 V.
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, both quoted as reduction potentials:
E°cell = (−1.18) − (+1.51) = −2.69 V
Do not multiply either value by 2 — electrode potential is an intensive property and does not
scale with the number of electrons, even though ΔG° does.
ΔG° = −nFE°cell, so a negative E°cell makes ΔG° positive.
∴ −2.69 V, and the reaction will not occur: it is non-spontaneous.

Conductivity and resistance are linked through the cell constant:
κ = G* / R, where G* = l/A is the cell constant in cm⁻¹.
Rearranging: G* = κ × R
Substitute the values given:
G* = 0.021 Ohm⁻¹ cm⁻¹ × 60 Ohm
G* = 1.26 cm⁻¹
The ohms cancel, leaving cm⁻¹, which is the right unit for a cell constant ✓.
The word 'centimolar' only tells you which standard KCl solution was used; it is not needed here.
∴ G* = 1.26 cm⁻¹.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|57||0|0.s:
For a first order reaction the integrated rate law is
ln[R] = ln[R]₀ − kt, equivalently log₁₀([R]₀/[R]) = kt/2.303.
Test each graph against that.
(2) ln[R] against t — the equation above is a straight line of slope −k ⇒ applicable.
(3) log₁₀[R] against t — the same line divided by 2.303, slope −k/2.303 ⇒ applicable.
(4) log₁₀([R]₀/[R]) against t — a straight line through the origin, slope k/2.303 ⇒ applicable.
(1) [R] against t drawn as a horizontal line would mean the concentration never changes.
For first order [R] = [R]₀e^(−kt), a falling exponential, never a constant.
A horizontal [R] against t is the graph of a zero order reaction's *rate*, not of a first order concentration.
∴ graph (1) is not applicable.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|58||0|0:
Each rate constant obeys Arrhenius: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT).
Substitute into the overall constant K = k₁k₂/k₃:
K = [A₁e^(−Ea₁/RT) × A₂e^(−Ea₂/RT)] / [A₃e^(−Ea₃/RT)]
Collect the exponentials, remembering that dividing subtracts the exponent:
K = (A₁A₂/A₃) · e^(−(Ea₁ + Ea₂ − Ea₃)/RT)
Comparing with K = Ae^(−Ea/RT), the overall activation energy is
Ea = Ea₁ + Ea₂ − Ea₃
Ea = 40 + 50 − 60 = 30 kJ mol⁻¹
The step in the denominator subtracts, because a larger k₃ makes K smaller.
∴ Ea = 30 kJ mol⁻¹.
